name: Mongolian urtiin duu long-song
lineage: Mongolian urtiin duu ("long song") tradition. Solo vocal art-form characterized by extreme melisma — single text syllables extended across many breaths in elaborate ornamental melodic territory, with characteristic falsetto-and-chest-register alternation, a vibrato called shuranhai produced by ornamental throat-tremolo, and an overall melodic range extending across two-and-a-half octaves. Repertoire draws on praise-songs to natural features (rivers, mountains, the eternal blue sky tngri), ancestor-veneration cycles, and ceremonial-occasion repertoire. Accompaniment on morin khuur (the two-string horsehead fiddle that is the canonical Mongolian instrument). Pentatonic modal vocabulary with mode-specific ornament conventions and a strongly pastoral-derived expressive register. Norovbanzad (1931-2002) is the twentieth-century canonical singer. Carole Pegg's Mongolian Music, Dance & Oral Narrative (University of Washington Press 2001) is the principal English-language scholarly documentation, with Mongolian National Folk Song and Dance Academy archives the institutional anchor. Distinguished from Mongolian bogino duu ("short song") by the long-song's extreme-melisma extended-form structure; distinguished from Tuvan ezengileer melodic-style by Mongolian-Khalkh dialect-specific cadential conventions; distinguished from Kazakh küy by voice-led (vs instrumental-led) tradition structure.
